text:
# How Git stores a commit

Every commit you make is stored as a handful of small files under `.git`. Git has three kinds of object that matter here (blobs, trees and commits) plus refs, which are the names that point at commits. Once you know how these four fit together, most of Git's behaviour stops being surprising.

## The object store

Everything Git remembers about your project's history lives in `.git/objects`. It is a key-value store: you hand Git some content, and Git gives back a 40-character hexadecimal ID, which is the SHA-1 hash of that content plus a short header. (Newer repositories can use SHA-256 instead; the design is the same.)

The ID is derived from the content, so the same content always gets the same ID, and an object can never change once written. Changing a byte would produce a different ID, which makes it a different object.

A new object is compressed with zlib and written to a file named after its ID. The first two characters become a directory and the remaining 38 the filename, so object `8ab686ea...` lives at `.git/objects/8a/b686ea...`. You can inspect any object with `git cat-file -p <id>`, and ask its type with `git cat-file -t <id>`.

## Blobs: file contents

A blob holds the contents of one file and nothing else. It has no filename, no permissions and no timestamp.

Two consequences follow. If the same file appears in ten directories, or stays unchanged across a thousand commits, Git stores one blob. And renaming a file creates no new blob, because the contents have not changed.

Blobs are created when you run `git add`, not when you commit. Staging a file writes its blob to the object store and records the blob's ID in the index (`.git/index`), which is the staging area.

## Trees: directories

A tree represents one directory. It is a list of entries, each with a mode, a type, an object ID and a name:

```
100644 blob 8ab686eafeb1f44702738c8b0f24f2567c36da6d    README.md
100755 blob 5e1c309dae7f45e0f39b1bf3ac3cd9db12e7d689    build.sh
040000 tree d8329fc1cc938780ffdd9f94e0d364e0ea74f579    src
```

This is where filenames live. The mode records whether an entry is a regular file, an executable, a symlink or a subdirectory. A subdirectory is an entry pointing at another tree, so one root tree describes the whole project at one moment.

Trees are content-addressed too. If nothing under `src/` changed between two commits, both root trees point at the same `src` tree object, and nothing new is stored for it.

## Commit objects

A commit is a small text object:

```
tree 4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904
parent a1b2c3d4e5f60718293a4b5c6d7e8f9012345678
author Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1762850000 +0000
committer Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1762850000 +0000

Fix off-by-one in pagination
```

It contains:

- **One tree ID**: the root tree, which is the complete state of the project at that commit.
- **Zero or more parent IDs**: none for the first commit, one for an ordinary commit, two or more for a merge.
- **Author and committer**: each with a name, an email and a timestamp.
- **The message**.

A commit stores a full snapshot, not a diff. When `git show` displays a diff, Git computes it on the spot by comparing the commit's tree with its parent's tree.

The parent ID is part of the commit's content, so it feeds into the commit's own ID. Each commit ID therefore depends on all the history before it. This is why amending or rebasing produces new commits with new IDs: the old commits are not edited, and they stay in the object store until garbage collection removes them.

When you run `git commit`, Git does three things:

1. It builds tree objects from the index, one per directory, reusing any that already exist.
2. It writes a commit object pointing at the root tree, with the current commit as parent.
3. It moves the current branch to the new commit.

## Refs: names for commits

Nobody wants to type 40-character IDs, so Git keeps refs. A ref is a file containing one commit ID. The branch `main` is the file `.git/refs/heads/main`, and its entire contents are 41 bytes: the ID and a newline.

- **Branches** live in `.git/refs/heads/`. Committing overwrites the file with the new commit's ID, so creating a branch costs one tiny file, however large the repository.
- **Remote-tracking branches** live in `.git/refs/remotes/`, and are updated by fetch and push.
- **Tags** live in `.git/refs/tags/`. A lightweight tag is a ref that never moves; an annotated tag points at a fourth object type, the tag object, which carries its own message and tagger.

`HEAD`, at `.git/HEAD`, records what you have checked out. It normally holds a reference to a branch, such as `ref: refs/heads/main`. In "detached HEAD" state, it holds a raw commit ID instead.

## Why you may not find these files

Storing every version of every file as its own compressed file would waste space. Periodically (`git gc`, which also runs automatically), Git gathers loose objects into packfiles under `.git/objects/pack/`, where similar objects are stored as deltas against one another. Refs get the same treatment and are collected into `.git/packed-refs`.

So in a mature repository, a branch or object may not exist as a file of its own. This is a storage optimisation only: `git cat-file` and `git rev-parse` behave the same either way, and every object is still a full snapshot as far as Git's model is concerned.

## See it yourself

In any repository, run:

```
cat .git/HEAD
git rev-parse HEAD
git cat-file -p HEAD
git cat-file -p 'HEAD^{tree}'
```

Then run `git cat-file -p` on one of the blob IDs from the last command, and you will have followed the chain from a ref to a commit, to a tree, to a file's contents.
